01
Chapter 1 · Spring Start Here

Spring in the real world

Why frameworks exist at all, what is actually inside the Spring ecosystem, where teams use it, and the four situations where reaching for it is a mistake.

📖 Book pages 3–21 🧩 8 figures Open chapter 1 PDF ↗
Start here

The chapter in one minute

Almost every application repeats the same non-business work: logging, security, transactions, talking to databases and other apps. A framework is a ready-made set of that work, so you write only what makes your app different.

If you remember only this

Spring is not a bag of magic tricks — it is plumbing you don't have to write. It gives your app a workshop full of parts (object management, web requests, database access, security, testing) and lets you assemble the ones you need.

Chapter 1 never asks you to code. It makes you choose Spring deliberately: know what it offers, know where it fits, and know when a plain Java class is the better answer.

01

Plumbing > business logic

In a typical app, the code for what the user wants is much smaller than the code that keeps the app alive. Frameworks supply the second part.

02

Spring is an ecosystem

Spring Core, Spring MVC, Spring Data Access and Spring testing sit inside the framework. Spring Boot, Spring Data and Spring Security are separate projects around it.

03

Inversion of control

Instead of your code creating and calling its dependencies, the framework creates and calls the parts you declare. That single flip is Spring's foundation.

04

Fit matters

Spring suits backend services, test automation, and even desktop or Android apps — but not tiny functions, locked-down security contexts, or an app that already works.

Section 1.1

Why should we use frameworks?

Because you have already solved most of your app's problems — in someone else's app.

What a framework actually is

An application framework is a set of common software functionalities that gives you a foundation to build on. It is not a library you call once; it is the skeleton your app hangs on. You don't have to use every feature it offers — you pick the parts your requirements need.

The wardrobe analogy (figure 1.1)

Image ordering a wardrobe from a DIY store. Normally you get exactly the panels and screws for that wardrobe, plus a manual. Now imagine the store instead delivers every part it sells — table legs, shelf brackets, hinges, wardrobe panels. Your wardrobe is in there, but you must find the right parts and assemble them.

That is a framework: it ships you far more capability than you will use, and it is your job to choose and assemble the right pieces into an app.

Why the idea appeared

Early applications were each unique and written from scratch. As more apps appeared, developers noticed they all had the same requirements. The book lists a few:

  • logging errors, warnings and info messages;
  • transactions, to keep data consistent (covered in chapter 13);
  • protection against the same common security vulnerabilities;
  • similar ways for applications to communicate with each other;
  • similar performance mechanisms, such as caching and data compression.

The list keeps going. The conclusion is blunt: the business logic of an app is significantly smaller than the "wheels and belts" that make its engine run — what developers call the plumbing.

What "business logic" means

The code that implements the user's expectations. "Clicking this link generates an invoice" is a use case; the code that does it is business logic. Everything else — security, logging, transactions — is supporting machinery. It is also the only part that makes two apps genuinely different.

Three reasons the trade is worth it

  1. Time and money. Reusing an implementation is cheaper than building it.
  2. Fewer bugs. Code that thousands of apps already run has been tested far more than your first draft.
  3. A community. When many developers use the same framework, someone has already hit your problem and written about it.

Here is that "iceberg" in Java. The first version is the plumbing every app needs, hand-written around four lines of real business logic. The second shows the same intent expressed with Spring annotations, which you will learn properly in chapters 4–6.

InvoiceService.javaDoing the plumbing yourself
public class InvoiceService {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(InvoiceService.class);
    private final DataSource dataSource;

    public InvoiceService(DataSource dataSource) {
        this.dataSource = dataSource;
    }

    public void createInvoice(Order order) {
        Connection connection = null;
        try {
            connection = dataSource.getConnection();
            connection.setAutoCommit(false);          // transaction: manual
            insertInvoice(connection, order);         // business logic
            insertLines(connection, order);           // business logic
            connection.commit();
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            rollbackQuietly(connection);              // transaction: manual
            log.error("Could not create invoice {}", order.id(), e); // logging: manual
            throw new IllegalStateException(e);
        } finally {
            closeQuietly(connection);                 // resource handling: manual
        }
    }
}

Notice what dominates: opening connections, committing, rolling back, closing, logging. The business logic is three lines. Multiply this by every service method and the iceberg becomes the whole app.

The book's warning

Using a framework is also a design and architecture decision, not just a dependency. It shapes how your app is put together — so learn the alternatives before you commit. Appendix A of the book covers software architecture in more depth.

Section 1.2

The Spring ecosystem

People say "the Spring framework", but what they really mean is a small solar system of projects, each solving one domain.

A story of transition (from the book)

The author joined a huge Java system that had grown into a "big ball of mud" over 25 years. Moving it to a modern architecture meant cleaning up the code, and the team chose Spring over Java EE because it was lighter, easier to implement and easier to maintain.

The transition was hard work — and it removed over 40% of the lines of code. That was the moment the impact of a framework became impossible to ignore.

Four parts inside the framework

PartWhat it gives youIn the book
Spring CoreThe foundation: the Spring context (which manages your object instances), aspects (which intercept and augment your methods), the Spring Expression Language (SpEL), resource management, type conversion and internationalization.Chapters 2–6
Spring MVCBuilds web applications and HTTP services in the classic servlet style.From chapter 7
Spring Data AccessTools to reach SQL databases: JDBC help, integration with ORM frameworks such as Hibernate, and transaction management.Chapters 12–14
Spring testingTools for unit and integration tests of Spring applications.Chapter 15

Picture Spring Core as the star in the middle, holding the other capabilities in orbit. Nothing works without it.

Projects around the framework

The ecosystem is larger than the framework itself. Each project is developed independently, by its own team, with its own reference documentation on spring.io/projects: Spring Boot, Spring Data, Spring Security, Spring Cloud, Spring Batch and many more. You can combine several in one app.

PROJECT

Spring Boot

Convention over configuration. Instead of configuring everything yourself, you accept a sensible default and change only what differs. Result: less code, faster starts.

PROJECT

Spring Data

A high-level layer over SQL and NoSQL databases so persistence takes a minimum of code (chapter 14).

Don't mix these two up

Spring Data Access is a module inside the framework: transactions, JDBC tools, ORM integration. Spring Data is a separate ecosystem project that layers convenience on top and spans different kinds of data sources. Similar names, different jobs.

The alternatives you should still consider

The book is careful here: there is no alternative to the whole ecosystem, but individual pieces have rivals. Jakarta EE offers CDI and EJB for object management and interceptors; Google Guice manages object instances in a container; Apache Shiro can replace Spring Security; the Play framework can replace Spring MVC; and Quarkus is a fast-maturing cloud-native option. The advice is to stay open-minded — no technology is "the one".

Section 1.2.1

Inversion of control — Spring's one big idea

Normally your code is in charge and calls its dependencies. With IoC, you hand that control to the framework, and it calls you.

Spring works on the principle of inversion of control. Through configuration, you tell the framework how to manage the code you wrote; the framework then decides when to create an instance or call a method. That is where the "inversion" comes from: the dependency controls the app, not the other way round.

The concrete piece that does this is the IoC container, which the book also calls the Spring context. You register objects with it ("make them known to Spring") and Spring then wires and manages them for you. Chapters 2–5 are entirely about it.

"Controls" is a precise word here

It means actions like creating an instance or calling a method. Spring can intercept a method and augment it — for example, log any error raised while that method runs. That interception capability is aspect-oriented programming (AOP), covered in chapter 6.

Side by side, in code

Same small app, two mindsets. First, you build the object graph by hand — every class, every constructor argument, every lifetime is your problem.

ManualWiring.javaWithout IoC
// You decide what exists, in what order, and who gets what.
var dataSource = new HikariDataSource(config);
var repository = new JdbcInvoiceRepository(dataSource);
var mailer     = new SmtpMailer("smtp.example.com", 587);
var service    = new InvoiceService(repository, mailer);

service.createInvoice(order);

Now you declare what you need and let the container assemble it. Classes announce their dependencies in a constructor; Spring supplies the rest.

ShopConfig.java + mainWith IoC
@Configuration
@ComponentScan("com.example.shop")
class ShopConfig {
}

@Service
class InvoiceService {
    private final InvoiceRepository repository;

    InvoiceService(InvoiceRepository repository) {   // Spring passes the dependency
        this.repository = repository;
    }

    public void createInvoice(Order order) {
        repository.save(Invoice.from(order));
    }
}

// Start the container once; everything declared above is wired for you.
try (var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(ShopConfig.class)) {
    var service = context.getBean(InvoiceService.class);
    service.createInvoice(order);
}

Nothing here is chapter 1 material to memorise — the book saves annotations for chapter 2. The point is the direction of control: your code stops calling the world into existence and starts describing what it needs.

Section 1.3

Where Spring actually gets used

Not only websites. The book names four real-world scenarios in which teams use Spring successfully.

1. Backend applications

A backend app runs on the server, manages data, and serves requests from client apps. Think of online banking: the mobile app and the website are clients; the backend manages accounts and transactions, stores data in databases, and talks to other backend systems.

This is where Spring's breadth pays off. Each label in the next figure is a different part of the ecosystem doing one job — and this is exactly what the rest of the book teaches.

2. Automation testing apps

Automated tests are software too. Teams build an app that validates every flow of the system under test, keep it in Git, and let a continuous integration tool such as Jenkins run it regularly and report failures. For complex systems, testing every flow by hand stops being an option.

Such a test app can be as complex as a backend: it connects to databases to verify data, messages queues to simulate scenarios, and calls REST endpoints. Spring is useful for all of that — the test frameworks themselves (Selenium, Cucumber, Gauge) sit alongside it.

3. Desktop apps & 4. Mobile apps

Desktop applications are rare now, but when you build one, the Spring context still gives you cleaner object management, plus caching or remote calls when needed. For mobile, the community project Spring for Android adds a REST client and authentication support for secured APIs.

Section 1.4

When not to use a framework

Using a tool that is too big for the job costs more energy and can give a worse result.

The chainsaw and the bread

You could cut bread with a chainsaw. It is harder, slower, more exhausting — and you may end up with breadcrumbs instead of slices. A knife is the right tool. The book lists four situations where a framework is the chainsaw.

SituationWhy the framework hurtsWhat it looks like
1. You need a tiny footprintContainers should be disposable and start fast. Every dependency adds weight and startup time.Serverless functions: tiny apps you barely control the deployment of, where a plain Java main is enough.
2. Security rules demand custom codeA public vulnerability in open source becomes public knowledge. Some organisations want the chance of exploitation near zero.Defence and governmental systems that require everything to be built in-house.
3. You'd customise everythingIf fitting the framework takes more code than writing the feature, you chose the wrong framework — or none.Components that don't fit and are patched, wrapped and overridden everywhere.
4. There's no real benefitRewriting something that already works adds risk and cost for no gain.Replacing a working setup because a new framework is popular.
The apparent contradiction, resolved

Earlier, open source was called more secure because a discovered vulnerability gets fixed publicly. Both are true. With enough time and money you can reach that standard yourself — it is simply more expensive. Most projects should use the framework; a few deliberately don't.

An avoidable mistake (from the book)

The team had ugly, hand-written JDBC everywhere. They wanted less code. The author suggested Spring's JdbcTemplate; others pushed for Hibernate because it was popular. After a proof of concept, two months of effort and a lot of stress, the team quit Hibernate and finished with JdbcTemplate — cleaner code, far fewer lines, no new framework.

The lesson: popularity is not a requirement. Ask what the change actually buys you. Jumping into it without a proof of concept is how good teams lose months.

This is what "no framework" can look like when it is the right call — the whole app, one file, no dependencies, starts instantly:

SlugFunction.javaWhen plain Java wins
import java.util.Locale;

/** A tiny function deployed in a container. A framework would only add weight. */
public final class SlugFunction {

    private SlugFunction() {
    }

    public static String apply(String title) {
        return title.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)
                    .trim()
                    .replaceAll("[^a-z0-9]+", "-")
                    .replaceAll("(^-|-$)", "");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(apply("  Spring in the Real World!  "));
        // spring-in-the-real-world
    }
}
Section 1.5

What you will be able to do after the book

The book assumes you know nothing about frameworks — and nothing about Spring.

It teaches the ecosystem, not only the core framework, and it deliberately doesn't follow a straight line: some ideas arrive early and only make sense once a few more puzzle pieces are in place. By the end you will be able to:

  • Use the Spring context and implement aspects around objects the framework manages.
  • Connect a Spring app to a database and work with persisted data.
  • Exchange data between apps over REST APIs built with Spring.
  • Build apps that use the convention-over-configuration approach.
  • Apply best practices to the standard class design of a Spring application.
  • Properly test your Spring implementations.
Companion

Every idea in this chapter, as code

Chapter 1 contains no listings of its own. These examples are written for this page so each figure has something concrete to point at — they are short, illustrative, and each one is annotated with the chapter where the book covers it properly.

The infrastructure Spring Boot removes

Figure 1.6 lists Spring Boot as "write less code to implement the app". The difference is easiest to see at the entry point: a servlet deployment needs wiring and a container; Boot needs one annotation and a main method.

ShopApplication.javaSpring Boot · ch. 7
@SpringBootApplication
public class ShopApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(ShopApplication.class, args);
    }
}

Backend: a REST endpoint (figure 1.6)

The client apps in figure 1.5 need something to call. A controller is a small class whose methods answer HTTP requests; Spring handles routing, JSON conversion and the servlet plumbing.

InvoiceController.javaSpring MVC · ch. 7
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/invoices")
public class InvoiceController {

    private final InvoiceRepository repository;

    public InvoiceController(InvoiceRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository;
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public InvoiceDto byId(@PathVariable long id) {
        return repository.findById(id)
                         .map(InvoiceDto::from)
                         .orElseThrow(() -> new ResponseStatusException(
                                 HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "No invoice " + id));
    }

    @GetMapping
    public List<InvoiceDto> byCustomer(@RequestParam long customerId) {
        return repository.findByCustomerId(customerId)
                         .stream()
                         .map(InvoiceDto::from)
                         .toList();
    }
}

Persistence: Spring Data vs Spring Data Access

The distinction from section 1.2 in one pair of examples. With Spring Data you declare an interface and Spring writes the implementation; the method name findByCustomerId is the query.

InvoiceRepository.javaSpring Data · ch. 14
public interface InvoiceRepository extends JpaRepository<Invoice, Long> {

    List<Invoice> findByCustomerId(long customerId);

    @Query("select sum(i.amount) from Invoice i where i.customerId = :customerId")
    BigDecimal totalFor(@Param("customerId") long customerId);
}

When you want the SQL in your own hands, Spring Data Access gives you the lower-level tool the book recommends for exactly that situation — JdbcTemplate, from the Hibernate story in section 1.4.

InvoiceReportDao.javaSpring Data Access · ch. 12
@Repository
public class InvoiceReportDao {

    private final JdbcTemplate jdbc;

    public InvoiceReportDao(JdbcTemplate jdbc) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
    }

    public BigDecimal totalFor(long customerId) {
        return jdbc.queryForObject("""
                select coalesce(sum(amount), 0)
                from invoice
                where customer_id = ?
                """, BigDecimal.class, customerId);
    }
}

Notice what disappeared

Compare this with the first listing on the page. Spring opens and closes the connection, participates in the transaction, and translates SQLExceptions. You still declare the boundary with @Transactional — the book's chapter 13 subject.

InvoiceService.javaTransactions + AOP · ch. 6, 13
@Service
public class InvoiceService {

    private final InvoiceRepository repository;

    public InvoiceService(InvoiceRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository;
    }

    @Transactional          // commit on success, roll back on any RuntimeException
    public void createInvoice(Order order) {
        repository.save(Invoice.from(order));
    }
}

And the logging that you wrote by hand in the first example becomes one method that applies to a whole package — this is the "aspecting" from figure 1.4, where Spring intercepts methods you define.

CallLoggingAspect.javaSpring AOP · ch. 6
@Aspect
@Component
public class CallLoggingAspect {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(CallLoggingAspect.class);

    @Before("execution(* com.example.shop.service.*.*(..))")
    public void logCall(JoinPoint call) {
        log.info("Calling {}", call.getSignature().toShortString());
    }
}

Testing: the confidence Figure 1.7 describes

Spring testing boots the parts of your app a test needs and injects them, so a test reads like the production flow instead of like setup code.

InvoiceServiceTests.javaSpring testing · ch. 15
@SpringBootTest
class InvoiceServiceTests {

    @Autowired
    InvoiceService service;

    @Test
    void rejectsAnEmptyOrder() {
        var order = new Order(1L, List.of());

        assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.createInvoice(order))
                .isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class);
    }
}
Hands-on

Try it in ten minutes

Chapter 1 is conceptual, so the exercise is to see the plumbing exist without writing it.

  1. Create a project at start.spring.io — Maven, Java 17 or newer — and add the Spring Web dependency.
  2. Add the controller and the ShopApplication class above.
  3. Run it and open http://localhost:8080/api/invoices. Look at the startup log: the container started, found your classes, and mapped the route — you wrote none of that.
  4. Delete @RestController and restart. The route is gone. That is control sitting with the framework, not with your code.

The only dependency you need for the web part:

pom.xmlSpring Boot parent required
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>
Keep it honest

After the exercise, ask the section 1.4 questions about your own project: does it deploy as a tiny container? Does it need a footprint this small? Do security rules force custom code? If the answers are "no", Spring is probably a good fit — and if the answers are "yes", you just saved a rewrite.

Recap

The chapter's summary, in plain sentences

Eight sentences worth remembering

  • A framework is a skeleton. It provides common functionalities and a foundation structure; you assemble your code onto it.
  • It saves time and bugs. Reuse beats rewriting, and widely used code has been tested by many teams.
  • The community is part of the value. Many developers understanding the same tool means your problem has probably been solved publicly.
  • Decide deliberately. Consider all possibilities — including no framework — and weigh purpose, community size and maturity.
  • Spring is an ecosystem. Spring Core, Spring MVC, Spring Data Access and Spring testing form the framework; Spring Boot, Spring Data, Spring Security and others are projects around it.
  • IoC is the foundation. The framework controls execution; you configure how your code is managed, and the Spring context is the container that does it.
  • It isn't only for websites. Backend apps, automation test apps, desktop apps and Android apps can all use Spring.
  • Sometimes you shouldn't. Tiny footprints, strict security, endless customisation, or no real benefit are all good reasons to stay with plain Java.

Four terms to carry into chapter 2

TermMeaning in one line
Business logicThe code implementing what the user actually wants; the only part that makes apps different.
PlumbingLogging, transactions, security, persistence, communication — the machinery every app needs.
IoC container / Spring contextThe part of Spring that creates, wires and manages the objects you register with it.
Convention over configurationAccept a sensible default, change only what differs — Spring Boot's core promise.

Chapter 2 · Spring Start Here

The Spring context: Defining beans

Spring starts out blind: it knows none of the objects you create. The context is the place you put the objects you want it to manage — and those managed objects are called beans. This chapter is about the three ways to get them in, and when each one is the right tool.

📖 Book pages 22–49 🧩 14 figures Open chapter 2 PDF ↗
Start here

The chapter in one minute

The context is a spot in your app's memory where the objects Spring should manage live. If an object isn't in there, Spring cannot see it, cannot wire it, and cannot add transactions, security or logging to it.

If you remember only this

Spring manages a bucket of objects, and you decide what goes in the bucket. Everything else in the framework — wiring, aspects, transactions, testing — works on the objects inside it. Chapter 1 explained why that is valuable; this chapter explains how to fill the bucket.

01

Empty by default

new Parrot() is invisible to Spring. Creating the context doesn't change that. You must add the instance.

02

Three doors

@Bean in a configuration class, stereotype annotations such as @Component, or a programmatic registerBean() call.

03

Names matter

Each bean gets an identifier: the @Bean method name by default, or a name you choose. You need it when several beans share a type.

04

Not everything

Only objects Spring must manage belong in the context. Adding every object is a common beginner mistake.

The one-sentence definition

A bean is simply an object instance that Spring created or accepted into its context, so the framework can manage it. It is not a special class, not a subclass, and not a different kind of object — just a normal Java object that Spring now knows about.

Section 2.1

A Maven project, in the few minutes it deserves

Maven has nothing to do with Spring itself. It is the build tool the book uses to download dependencies, and you only need its basics to follow along.

A build tool is software you configure once to perform the tasks that are part of building an app, instead of doing them by hand. The book lists the usual tasks:

  • downloading the dependencies your app needs;
  • running tests;
  • validating that the syntax follows the rules you define;
  • checking for security vulnerabilities;
  • compiling the app;
  • packaging it into an executable archive.

The book uses IntelliJ IDEA, but stresses that the project structure is the same in Eclipse, Spring STS, NetBeans or anything else. When you create the project you choose Maven in the left panel and pick your JDK; in the next window you give it a name and, optionally, three coordinates:

  • group ID — groups several related projects;
  • artifact ID — the name of this application;
  • version — an identifier of this implementation state.

Once the project exists, its structure is always the same two things: an src folder holding everything that belongs to the app, and a pom.xml file holding the project's configuration — above all, its dependencies.

sq-ch2-ex1/ ├── src/ │ ├── main/ │ │ ├── java/ ← your application code │ │ └── resources/ ← properties and configuration files │ └── test/ │ └── java/ ← unit tests (chapter 15) └── pom.xml ← build configuration and dependencies

The pom.xml file

Immediately after creation, the file declares the project coordinates and nothing else. With this content the project uses no external dependency at all — only the JDK.

pom.xmlListing 2.1 · default content
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0
         http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">

  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
  <groupId>org.example</groupId>
  <artifactId>sq-ch2-ex1</artifactId>
  <version>1.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</project>

Dependencies go between <dependencies> tags, each described by group ID, artifact name and version. Maven looks them up, by default in the Maven Central repository, and downloads the jars into your project.

pom.xmlListing 2.2 · adding a dependency
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-jdbc</artifactId>
      <version>5.2.6.RELEASE</version>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>

The dependency you actually need for this chapter

Spring is modular: you add only the parts you use, never "all of Spring". For this chapter that means one artifact, spring-context, which pulls in what the context needs.

pom.xmlListing 2.5 · Spring context dependency
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
      <version>5.2.6.RELEASE</version>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
How to find a dependency without memorising it

Search the Spring reference documentation — Spring artifacts almost always live under the org.springframework group ID. The book's author knows these by heart, and says plainly that you don't need to. Version note: the book uses 5.2.6.RELEASE because that was current when it was written; with Spring Boot you would normally let a parent POM choose the version for you.

Section 2.2

Adding beans to the Spring context

Three ways, one goal: make Spring aware of an object so the framework can manage it.

@Bean in a configuration class Stereotype annotations (@Component) Programmatically with registerBean()

The book builds one skeleton project first — no framework at all — to make the starting point obvious: a plain Parrot class with a name, and a Main that creates an instance.

Parrot.javaListing 2.3 · plain Java object
public class Parrot {

    private String name;

    // Omitted getters and setters
}
Main.javaListings 2.4 & 2.6 · before Spring
public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext();  // empty context
        Parrot p = new Parrot();                                // not a bean yet
    }
}

The context exists. The parrot exists. They have never met — and that is exactly the problem the rest of the chapter solves.

Why AnnotationConfigApplicationContext?

Spring offers several context implementations. This one uses annotations — today's dominant style — so it is the one the book uses throughout. The author explicitly advises not to dig into the inheritance chains of context implementations while learning: you would lose time on details that don't matter yet.

Section 2.2.1

Way 1 — the @Bean annotation

The most explicit option: you write a method that builds the object, and Spring calls it for you.

This approach works for classes you wrote and for classes you didn't — anything you can construct in Java can become a bean. Three steps:

  1. Define a configuration class

    Annotate a class with @Configuration. Configuration classes are where you tell Spring what to do.

  2. Add a method that returns the instance

    Annotate it with @Bean. Spring calls this method when it initialises the context and puts the returned value into it.

  3. Make Spring use that configuration class

    Pass it to the context constructor: new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(ProjectConfig.class).

ProjectConfig.javaListing 2.8
@Configuration
public class ProjectConfig {

    @Bean
    Parrot parrot() {
        var p = new Parrot();
        p.setName("Koko");
        return p;
    }
}
Main.javaListings 2.9 & 2.10
public class Main {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(
        ProjectConfig.class);

    Parrot p = context.getBean(Parrot.class);
    System.out.println(p.getName());   // Koko
  }
}
ConsoleKoko

Why the method name has no verb

Java convention says methods are actions, so they get verbs. @Bean methods break that rule on purpose: a method like parrot() represents the object it returns, and its name becomes the bean's identifier in the context. Use a noun — usually the class name, lower-cased.

Any object can be a bean

Nothing restricts beans to your own classes. The book adds a String and an Integer to prove the point.

ProjectConfig.javaListing 2.11 · three beans, three types
@Configuration
public class ProjectConfig {

    @Bean
    Parrot parrot() {
        var p = new Parrot();
        p.setName("Koko");
        return p;
    }

    @Bean
    String hello() {
        return "Hello";
    }

    @Bean
    Integer ten() {
        return 10;
    }
}
Main.javaListing 2.12 · getBean by type
var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(ProjectConfig.class);

Parrot p = context.getBean(Parrot.class);
System.out.println(p.getName());      // Koko

String s = context.getBean(String.class);
System.out.println(s);                // Hello

Integer n = context.getBean(Integer.class);
System.out.println(n);                // 10

No casting needed: getBean(Class) looks up a bean of exactly that type. If none exists, Spring throws an exception rather than returning null.

Several beans of the same type

Declare more @Bean methods returning the same type and you get several instances — each with its own identifier. The parrot's name ("Koko") is just an attribute; the bean name is the method name ("parrot1"). Spring cares only about the latter.

ProjectConfig.javaListing 2.13 · three parrots
@Configuration
public class ProjectConfig {

    @Bean
    Parrot parrot1() {
        var p = new Parrot();
        p.setName("Koko");
        return p;
    }

    @Bean
    Parrot parrot2() {
        var p = new Parrot();
        p.setName("Miki");
        return p;
    }

    @Bean
    Parrot parrot3() {
        var p = new Parrot();
        p.setName("Riki");
        return p;
    }
}

Asking by type alone now fails — Spring cannot guess which of the three you mean:

Exception · asking for Parrot.class with three candidatesException in thread "main" org.springframework.beans.factory.NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException: No qualifying bean of type 'main.Parrot' available: expected single matching bean but found 3: parrot1,parrot2,parrot3
Main.javaListing 2.15 · by identifier
Parrot p = context.getBean("parrot2", Parrot.class);
System.out.println(p.getName());   // Miki
ProjectConfig.javaRenaming a bean
@Bean(name = "miki")      // or @Bean(value = "miki")
Parrot parrot2() {        // or @Bean("miki")
    var p = new Parrot();
    p.setName("Miki");
    return p;
}

Making one bean the default: @Primary

If you have several beans of a type but usually want one, mark it @Primary. It becomes Spring's choice whenever you don't name a bean explicitly. Only one bean per type can be primary.

ProjectConfig.java@Primary · the default choice
@Bean
@Primary
Parrot parrot2() {
    var p = new Parrot();
    p.setName("Miki");
    return p;
}

// Now context.getBean(Parrot.class) returns Miki, no exception.
Section 2.2.2

Way 2 — stereotype annotations

Put an annotation on the class and let Spring create the instance. Less code, less control.

Spring offers several stereotype annotations; the book starts with the most basic, @Component. Marking a class as a component tells Spring: when the context initialises, create an instance of this class and add it. But Spring does not scan for these annotations by default — you must also say where to look.

  1. Annotate the class with @Component

    This is the class you want an instance of in the context.

  2. Annotate the configuration class with @ComponentScan

    Point it at the packages containing your annotated classes, e.g. @ComponentScan(basePackages = "main").

Parrot.javaListing 2.16
@Component
public class Parrot {

    private String name;

    public String getName() { return name; }
    public void setName(String name) { this.name = name; }
}
ProjectConfig.javaListing 2.17
@Configuration
@ComponentScan(basePackages = "main")
public class ProjectConfig {
    // no bean methods at all
}

No methods, no new, no wiring code — and the bean still appears. What you lose is the chance to configure the object while creating it:

Main.javaListing 2.18 · the catch
var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(ProjectConfig.class);
Parrot p = context.getBean(Parrot.class);

System.out.println(p);          // main.Parrot@1b6d3586  ← the bean exists
System.out.println(p.getName()); // null  ← nobody called setName
This is the trade-off in one line

With @Component, Spring creates the object using its constructor and hands it over as-is. If the object needs a starting value or extra setup, you have to do it after creation — with @PostConstruct.

Running code right after creation: @PostConstruct

Annotate a method in the component class and Spring calls it once the constructor has finished. The book borrows this annotation from Java EE, so on Java 11+ it needs an explicit dependency — the Java EE APIs were removed from the JDK in 11.

pom.xmlNeeded on Java 11+
<dependency>
  <groupId>javax.annotation</groupId>
  <artifactId>javax.annotation-api</artifactId>
  <version>1.3.2</version>
</dependency>
Parrot.java@PostConstruct
@Component
public class Parrot {

    private String name;

    @PostConstruct
    public void init() {
        this.name = "Kiki";
    }

    // Omitted getters and setters
}

Print the name now and you get Kiki. Modern note: Spring 6 and Spring Boot 3 moved to jakarta.annotation, so on current versions the dependency and import are jakarta.annotation-api / jakarta.annotation.PostConstruct instead of javax.

@PreDestroy — the book advises against it

It exists, and Spring calls the annotated method just before closing the context. But the author recommends avoiding it: context cleanup can fail or not happen, and if you put something critical there — closing a database connection, say — you may end up in serious trouble. Use an explicit, reliable mechanism instead.

Table 2.1 — the two annotation approaches compared

Using @BeanUsing stereotype annotations
Full control over instance creation: you build and configure it in the method; Spring adds it as-is.You control the instance only after the framework creates it.
You can add several beans of the same type (parrot1, parrot2, parrot3).One instance of the class per context.
You can add any object — the class doesn't have to live in your app (a String, an Integer, a library type).Only classes your application owns, because you must edit the class to annotate it.
One method per bean: boilerplate. The book treats it as the second choice.No boilerplate. The preferred choice for your own classes.

Which is why the book's rule of thumb is simple: use stereotype annotations as much as possible, and @Bean when you cannot annotate the class.

Section 2.2.3

Way 3 — adding beans programmatically

When the decision depends on something that only exists at runtime, call registerBean().

Available since Spring 5, this approach lets you add instances by calling a method on the context itself. Annotations are declarative — fixed at compile time — so they cannot express a choice like this:

The case annotations cannot expressRuntime choice
if (condition) {
    registerBean(b1);
} else {
    registerBean(b2);
}

The book's example: the app reads a collection of parrots, some green and some orange, and only the green ones should become beans.

The method takes four parameters, the last of which is optional:

ApplicationContext.javaregisterBean signature
<T> void registerBean(
    String beanName,                          // null if you don't need a name
    Class<T> beanClass,                       // e.g. Parrot.class
    Supplier<T> supplier,                     // returns the instance to add
    BeanDefinitionCustomizer... customizers); // optional: make it primary, etc.

A Supplier is the functional interface from java.util.function that returns a value without taking arguments — so a lambda that hands back your object is exactly enough.

Main.javaListing 2.19 · registerBean
public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(ProjectConfig.class);

        Parrot x = new Parrot();          // 1. create the instance
        x.setName("Kiki");

        Supplier<Parrot> parrotSupplier = () -> x;   // 2. wrap it in a Supplier

        context.registerBean("parrot1", Parrot.class, parrotSupplier);  // 3. register

        Parrot p = context.getBean(Parrot.class);
        System.out.println(p.getName());  // Kiki
    }
}

The configuration class stays empty and Parrot stays a plain object — no annotations anywhere. Because the last parameter is a varargs of customisers, you can also set characteristics such as primacy:

Main.javaBeanDefinitionCustomizer · primary
context.registerBean("parrot1",
        Parrot.class,
        parrotSupplier,
        bc -> bc.setPrimary(true));
When not to reach for this

It is the most flexible option and also the most manual: nothing in the code tells a reader that the bean exists unless they read main. Use it for conditional or dynamically driven registration; use annotations for the stable, structural parts of your app.

Decision guide

Which approach should you use?

Three questions, in order. The first "yes" wins.

01

Does the class belong to you?

Then put @Component on it and @ComponentScan on a configuration class. This is the everyday default: least code, easiest to read.

02

Is it a class you cannot edit?

A library type, a framework class, or a value like a String. You cannot annotate it, so declare it with @Bean — full control over how it is built.

03

Do you need several of them?

Several instances of one type, each configured differently: @Bean methods, one per instance, with their own identifiers.

04

Does the choice happen at runtime?

Which beans to add depends on data, configuration or a condition: context.registerBean() inside your own logic.

In practice they mix. A configuration class can declare beans for library types while your own services carry stereotype annotations — the book starts combining them from chapter 4 onwards:

ShopConfig.javaBoth approaches in one app
@Configuration
@ComponentScan(basePackages = "com.example.shop")   // your own classes arrive here
public class ShopConfig {

    @Bean
    DataSource dataSource() {                        // a library type: you own it
        var ds = new HikariDataSource();
        ds.setJdbcUrl("jdbc:h2:mem:shop");
        return ds;
    }
}
The mental model to keep

Annotations are how you label things that are already yours. @Bean is how you manufacture something that isn't. registerBean() is how you decide at runtime what goes in the box. All three end in the same place — the context.

Recap

Chapter 2's summary, in plain sentences

Five sentences worth remembering

  • The context is a bucket. Add the instances you expect Spring to manage; Spring can see only what is inside.
  • Three ways in. @Bean, stereotype annotations, or registerBean().
  • @Bean is the flexible one. Any object, any number of instances of a type, full control over creation — but one method per bean.
  • Stereotypes are the convenient one. Less code for classes you own, one instance per class, and @PostConstruct if you need to configure it afterwards.
  • registerBean() is the dynamic one. Spring 5 and later, for decisions annotations cannot express.

What changed in your head

At the end of chapter 1 you knew why a framework exists. Now you know the mechanism Spring is built on: a context full of beans, which you populate deliberately. Being able to put objects in is the prerequisite for everything that follows — because chapter 3 is about what those beans can do for each other.

Chapter 3 wires beans together: how one bean gets a reference to another, and how Spring resolves dependencies you never pass explicitly.

Chapter 3 · Spring Start Here

The Spring context: Wiring beans

Chapter 2 filled the bucket. Now the beans have to talk to each other: one object holds a reference to another so it can delegate work. This chapter covers the ways to establish those links, how Spring injects values, what breaks when dependencies point in a circle, and how to pick one bean when several share a type.

📖 Book pages 50–74 🧩 13 figures Open chapter 3 PDF ↗
Start here

The chapter in one minute

Calling getBean() everywhere is not how applications are written. Beans need references to each other — and Spring's job is to supply them.

If you remember only this

Wiring is how one bean gets a reference to another. You can link beans by calling the other @Bean method directly, by declaring a method parameter and letting Spring fill it, or by annotating a field, constructor or setter with @Autowired.

Everything in this chapter is really one idea — dependency injection — seen from four angles: how it is declared, why the constructor version is the one to use, what happens when it becomes circular, and how Spring chooses when it has too many candidates.

01

A "has-A" link

A Person bean owns a Parrot bean. Until you wire them, person.getParrot() is null.

02

Three doors again

Direct call in the config class, method parameter, or @Autowired on a field / constructor / setter.

03

Circles fail

Two beans that need each other deadlock Spring at startup. It is a design problem, not a Spring limitation.

04

Names resolve ties

With several candidates, Spring matches the parameter name, then honours @Primary, then @Qualifier.

Section 3.1

Relationships between beans defined with @Bean

Two beans in the context, one relationship to create. The book's example is deliberately small: a person who owns a parrot.

In object-oriented code, objects delegate responsibilities to other objects. Spring does not remove that need; it just supplies the references. The relationship is a plain "has-A": Person has a Parrot field.

  1. Add both beans to the context

    One @Bean method for the parrot, one for the person — as you learned in chapter 2.

  2. Establish the relationship

    Either call the parrot() method from person() (wiring), or let Spring pass the parrot in as a parameter (auto-wiring).

Start with the two classes and two beans, and nothing linking them:

Parrot.javachapter 3 model
public class Parrot {

    private String name;

    // Omitted getters and setters

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "Parrot : " + name;
    }
}
Person.javachapter 3 model
public class Person {

    private String name;
    private Parrot parrot;

    // Omitted getters and setters
}
ProjectConfig.javaListing 3.1 · two beans, no link
@Configuration
public class ProjectConfig {

    @Bean
    public Parrot parrot() {
        Parrot p = new Parrot();
        p.setName("Koko");
        return p;
    }

    @Bean
    public Person person() {
        Person p = new Person();
        p.setName("Ella");
        return p;
    }
}
Main.javaListing 3.2 · checking for a link
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(ProjectConfig.class);

        Person person = context.getBean(Person.class);
        Parrot parrot = context.getBean(Parrot.class);

        System.out.println("Person's name: " + person.getName());
        System.out.println("Parrot's name: " + parrot.getName());
        System.out.println("Person's parrot: " + person.getParrot());
    }
}
Console · the third line is the pointPerson's name: Ella Parrot's name: Koko Person's parrot: null

Both beans exist. Neither knows the other. null is the honest answer, and it is exactly what the rest of the chapter fixes.

Section 3.1.1

Wiring by calling the other @Bean method

One extra line in the configuration class: p.setParrot(parrot()).

ProjectConfig.javaListing 3.3 · direct wiring
@Configuration
public class ProjectConfig {

    @Bean
    public Parrot parrot() {
        Parrot p = new Parrot();
        p.setName("Koko");
        return p;
    }

    @Bean
    public Person person() {
        Person p = new Person();
        p.setName("Ella");
        p.setParrot(parrot());   // ← the link
        return p;
    }
}
Console · same app, one line laterPerson's name: Ella Person's parrot: Parrot : Koko

"Does this create a second parrot?"

This is the question the author hears in every class, and the answer is no. Spring controls how @Bean methods are called — the same interception mechanism that appears again in chapter 6. When person() calls parrot(), Spring does not run the method body again if the bean already exists.

You can prove it yourself. Add a no-args constructor that prints, and count the messages:

Parrot.javathe experiment
public class Parrot {

    private String name;

    public Parrot() {
        System.out.println("Parrot created");
    }

    // Omitted getters and setters
}
Console · printed once, so only one parrot existsParrot created Person's name: Ella Person's parrot: Parrot : Koko
Section 3.1.2

Wiring through a @Bean method's parameter

Instead of calling the method, ask for the bean as an argument. Spring finds it and passes it in.

ProjectConfig.javaListing 3.4 · parameter injection
@Configuration
public class ProjectConfig {

    @Bean
    public Parrot parrot() {
        Parrot p = new Parrot();
        p.setName("Koko");
        return p;
    }

    @Bean
    public Person person(Parrot parrot) {   // ← Spring supplies this argument
        Person p = new Person();
        p.setName("Ella");
        p.setParrot(parrot);
        return p;
    }
}

This version is slightly more flexible than the direct call: the parrot bean can come from a @Bean method or from a stereotype annotation, and this code would not change. In practice, the book notes, developers mostly choose between the two styles by taste — you will meet both, so know both.

This is dependency injection

Dependency injection is the technique where the framework sets a value into a field or parameter for you. It is a direct application of the inversion of control from chapter 1: your code no longer creates its collaborators, it declares them and receives them.

Section 3.2

Injecting with @Autowired

Move the intention out of the configuration class and into the class that needs the dependency.

This is the approach you reach for when you can edit the class — which, for your own classes, is almost always. Instead of a configuration method handing over the dependency, the class itself says "inject here". The relationship becomes visible where the field is declared, which many developers find easier to read than looking up a configuration class.

There are three places to put it, and they are not equally good:

Field — common in examples Constructor — the production choice Setter — rare, not recommended
Section 3.2.1

Field injection

The shortest version, and the one with the most caveats.

Parrot.java@Component
@Component
public class Parrot {

    private String name = "Koko";

    // Omitted getters and setters

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "Parrot : " + name;
    }
}
Person.java@Autowired on the field
@Component
public class Person {

    private String name = "Ella";

    @Autowired
    private Parrot parrot;

    // Omitted getters and setters
}
ProjectConfig.java & Main.javascanning + proof
@Configuration
@ComponentScan(basePackages = "beans")
public class ProjectConfig {
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(ProjectConfig.class);
        Person p = context.getBean(Person.class);

        System.out.println("Person's name: " + p.getName());
        System.out.println("Person's parrot: " + p.getParrot());
    }
}
ConsolePerson's name: Ella Person's parrot: Parrot : Koko
Why not field injection in production

Two concrete problems: the field cannot be final (a final field needs an initial value, and Spring sets it after construction — the book shows that this does not compile), and you lose easy control of the object at construction time, which matters when you create instances yourself in tests. It is fine for examples and proofs of concept, which is where you mostly see it.

Section 3.2.2

Constructor injection — the one to default to

Same result, but the field can be final and the object is valid the moment it exists.

Person.javaListing 3.5 · constructor injection
@Component
public class Person {

    private String name = "Ella";
    private final Parrot parrot;          // can be final now

    @Autowired
    public Person(Parrot parrot) {
        this.parrot = parrot;
    }

    // Omitted getters and setters
}
Small shortcut worth knowing

Since Spring 4.3, if the class has exactly one constructor, you can leave the @Autowired annotation off entirely — Spring will use that constructor anyway. The book annotates it to make the intention explicit.

The output is identical to the field version. What changes is what you can do with the class afterwards: it can be final-safe, and a unit test can simply write new Person(new Parrot()) without Spring at all.

Section 3.2.3

Setter injection

Mentioned for completeness, not as advice.

Person.java@Autowired on the setter
@Component
public class Person {

    private String name = "Ella";
    private Parrot parrot;

    @Autowired
    public void setParrot(Parrot parrot) {
        this.parrot = parrot;
    }
}

It works and the output is the same, but it has more disadvantages than advantages: harder to read, the field cannot be final, and it does not help testing. The author has seen it only in a couple of old applications — worth recognising, not worth choosing.

Where @Autowired goesVerdict in the bookWhy
FieldExamples and proofs of conceptShortest to write; field can't be final; harder to manage at initialisation and in tests.
ConstructorUse this in real codeFields can be final; object is complete when created; trivial to unit-test without Spring.
SetterRarely, avoidNo final, less readable, no testing benefit.
Section 3.3

Circular dependencies

If A needs B and B needs A, nobody can be built first. Spring stops with an exception — and that is the correct behaviour.

Person.javaneeds a Parrot
@Component
public class Person {

    private final Parrot parrot;

    @Autowired
    public Person(Parrot parrot) {
        this.parrot = parrot;
    }
}
Parrot.javaneeds a Person
@Component
public class Parrot {

    private final Person person;

    @Autowired
    public Parrot(Person person) {
        this.person = person;
    }
}
Exception · the app does not startCaused by: org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanCurrentlyInCreationException: Error creating bean with name 'parrot': Requested bean is currently in creation: Is there an unresolvable circular reference? at org.springframework.beans.factory.support.DefaultSingletonBeanRegistry .beforeSingletonCreation(DefaultSingletonBeanRegistry.java:347)
How to fix it (and how not to)

The fix is design, not annotation: remove the cycle. If a parrot truly needs a person and a person truly needs a parrot, the responsibilities are tangled — extract the shared behaviour into a third class that both can use. The book is blunt that circular dependencies come from bad class design, and that every Spring developer creates one at least once. When you see this exception, go to the classes it names and break the loop.

Section 3.4

Choosing between beans of the same type

Three parrots, one parameter. Spring resolves the ambiguity in a fixed order.

  1. The parameter name matches a bean name

    Spring injects the bean whose identifier equals the parameter's name. Convenient, but a rename can silently change behaviour.

  2. Otherwise, a primary bean wins

    If you marked one with @Primary (chapter 2), that is the default choice.

  3. Otherwise, ask for one explicitly

    @Qualifier("parrot2") names the bean you want.

  4. Otherwise: failure

    No match, no primary, no qualifier — the context cannot start because Spring refuses to guess.

ProjectConfig.javaListing 3.6 · matching by parameter name
@Configuration
public class ProjectConfig {

    @Bean
    public Parrot parrot1() {
        Parrot p = new Parrot();
        p.setName("Koko");
        return p;
    }

    @Bean
    public Parrot parrot2() {
        Parrot p = new Parrot();
        p.setName("Miki");
        return p;
    }

    @Bean
    public Person person(Parrot parrot2) {   // name decides: Miki, not Koko
        Person p = new Person();
        p.setName("Ella");
        p.setParrot(parrot2);
        return p;
    }
}
ConsoleParrot created Person's name: Ella Person's parrot: Parrot : Miki
The book prefers being explicit

Parameter names are easy to change during a refactor — and then the app silently wires a different bean. @Qualifier states the intention in a way a rename cannot break. Developers do argue about whether it is boilerplate; the author's position is that clarity wins.

ProjectConfig.javaListing 3.7 · @Qualifier
    @Bean
    public Person person(@Qualifier("parrot2") Parrot parrot) {
        Person p = new Person();
        p.setName("Ella");
        p.setParrot(parrot);
        return p;
    }

The same problem appears with @Autowired, and the same answer applies. Here Person is a component whose constructor takes a parrot, while the two parrots are declared with @Bean:

Person.javaparameter named parrot2
@Component
public class Person {

    private String name = "Ella";
    private final Parrot parrot;

    public Person(Parrot parrot2) {
        this.parrot = parrot2;
    }
}
ProjectConfig.javaListing 3.8 · two parrots
@Configuration
@ComponentScan(basePackages = "beans")
public class ProjectConfig {

    @Bean
    public Parrot parrot1() {
        Parrot p = new Parrot();
        p.setName("Koko");
        return p;
    }

    @Bean
    public Parrot parrot2() {
        Parrot p = new Parrot();
        p.setName("Miki");
        return p;
    }
}
Person.java@Qualifier in the constructor
@Component
public class Person {

    private String name = "Ella";
    private final Parrot parrot;

    public Person(@Qualifier("parrot2") Parrot parrot) {
        this.parrot = parrot;
    }
}

Same behaviour, less fragile code. That is the pattern to take into real projects: name the intent, not the variable.

Recap

Chapter 3's summary, in plain sentences

Seven sentences worth remembering

  • Beans must be linked. An object delegates to others, so the context has to supply those references.
  • Three routes. Call the @Bean method directly, declare a method parameter, or use @Autowired on a field, constructor or setter.
  • Spring intercepts @Bean calls. Calling parrot() returns the existing bean; it does not build a second parrot.
  • Injection is IoC in action. The framework sets the value; your code only declares what it needs.
  • Prefer constructor injection. Final fields, complete objects, easy tests. Field injection is for examples; setter injection is legacy.
  • Circles are a design smell. Spring fails fast with BeanCurrentlyInCreationException; untangle the classes.
  • Be explicit when choosing. Parameter names work, but @Qualifier survives refactoring; @Primary is the fallback default.

What changed in your head

Chapter 2 made objects visible to Spring. Chapter 3 made them useful to each other — which means you can now build a small object graph and let the framework assemble it. What is still missing is the reason real code rarely wires concrete classes directly: abstractions.

Chapter 4 introduces interfaces into the picture: how Spring injects a contract rather than a class, and why that keeps an app testable and easy to change.

Chapter 4 · Spring Start Here

The Spring context: Using abstractions

Real applications do not wire concrete classes to concrete classes. They depend on interfaces — contracts that say what is needed without saying how it is done. This chapter builds a realistic class design, then shows how Spring injects by contract, picks between implementations, and how @Service and @Repository make responsibilities visible.

📖 Book pages 75–98 🧩 12 figures Open chapter 4 PDF ↗
Start here

The chapter in one minute

Depend on the job description, not the person doing it. In Java that means depend on an interface, and let Spring decide which implementation to hand you.

If you remember only this

An interface is a contract: it states the what; implementations define the how. If CommentService needs something that can store a comment, it should ask for CommentRepository — not for DBCommentRepository. Then the storage can change to a different database, an external service, or a test double without touching the service.

Spring understands abstractions: when a bean needs a CommentRepository, Spring finds the bean built from a class that implements it. This is the shape almost every real Spring app has.

01

Interfaces decouple

Changing an implementation should not force changes in the object that uses it.

02

Only some objects are beans

Add an object to the context if it has an injected dependency or is one. Not every object.

03

Never annotate interfaces

Stereotypes go on classes — the things Spring can instantiate.

04

Name the responsibility

@Service and @Repository are @Component with meaning: they document the class design.

Section 4.1

Interfaces define contracts

"What needs to happen" belongs in the interface. " How it happens" belongs to whoever implements it.

Two analogies from the book

The screwdriver. As a child, the author wanted to open a radio case and asked his father for a knife. His father asked what he needed it for, then handed him a screwdriver instead. The lesson: ask for what you need, not for a solution you guessed at. An interface is how an object asks for what it needs.

The ride-sharing app. You request a trip, not a specific car or driver. The app is the interface: you and the driver are decoupled, and any driver able to provide the service can answer. You never learn who picked you up until they arrive.

The problem: strong coupling

A DeliveryDetailsPrinter must print delivery details sorted by destination address, so it delegates the sorting to a SorterByAddress object. That works — until the business asks for sorting by sender name. Now you must write a new sorter and change the printer that used the old one.

DeliveryDetailsPrinter.javatightly coupled
public class DeliveryDetailsPrinter {

    private SorterByAddress sorter;   // ← a concrete class

    public DeliveryDetailsPrinter(SorterByAddress sorter) {
        this.sorter = sorter;
    }

    public void printDetails() {
        sorter.sortDetails();
        // printing the delivery details
    }
}
The cost of that choicefigure 4.2
// Sorting must change from address to sender name:
//   1. write a new SorterByName class
//   2. change DeliveryDetailsPrinter to accept it
//
// The printer has no interest in *how* sorting happens,
// yet it must change when that how changes.

The fix: depend on the interface

Introduce a Sorter interface. The printer now declares that it needs a sorter; any class implementing the contract can satisfy it, now or later.

Sorter.java + DeliveryDetailsPrinter.javadecoupled by a contract
public interface Sorter {
    void sortDetails();
}

public class DeliveryDetailsPrinter {

    private Sorter sorter;            // ← the contract, not a class

    public DeliveryDetailsPrinter(Sorter sorter) {
        this.sorter = sorter;
    }

    public void printDetails() {
        sorter.sortDetails();
        // printing the delivery details
    }
}
Section 4.1.2

A requirement that looks like real work

A task-management app. A user publishes a comment on a task: the comment is stored, and an email notification is sent to a configured address.

Two actions, different in nature, so two responsibilities. Following the naming conventions the book describes:

  • CommentService — implements the publish comment use case. Service classes get names ending in "service" so their role is obvious.
  • CommentRepository — stores the comment. Objects working directly with a database are called repositories (sometimes data access objects, DAOs).
  • CommentNotificationProxy — talks to something outside the app, so it is named a proxy. Today it sends email; tomorrow it might be push or SMS.
  • Comment — a plain POJO with an author and a text. Objects that only model data are called models.

Design them as contracts

Both collaborators should be interfaces. Storage will change eventually; so will the notification channel. The service must not care.

Section 4.1.3

Building it without a framework first

One package per responsibility, no dependencies in the pom — plain Java, so the wiring is visible.

model/Comment.javaListing 4.1 · the POJO
public class Comment {

    private String author;
    private String text;

    // Omitted getters and setters
}
repositories/CommentRepository.javaListing 4.2 · the contract
public interface CommentRepository {

    void storeComment(Comment comment);   // the "what"
}
repositories/DBCommentRepository.javaListing 4.3 · the "how"
public class DBCommentRepository implements CommentRepository {

    @Override
    public void storeComment(Comment comment) {
        // A real database arrives in chapter 12; for now, simulate it.
        System.out.println("Storing comment: " + comment.getText());
    }
}
proxies/CommentNotificationProxy.javaListing 4.4
public interface CommentNotificationProxy {

    void sendComment(Comment comment);
}
proxies/EmailCommentNotificationProxy.javaListing 4.5
public class EmailCommentNotificationProxy
        implements CommentNotificationProxy {

    @Override
    public void sendComment(Comment comment) {
        System.out.println("Sending notification for comment: "
                + comment.getText());
    }
}
services/CommentService.javaListing 4.6 · the use case
public class CommentService {

    private final CommentRepository commentRepository;
    private final CommentNotificationProxy commentNotificationProxy;

    public CommentService(CommentRepository commentRepository,
                          CommentNotificationProxy commentNotificationProxy) {
        this.commentRepository = commentRepository;
        this.commentNotificationProxy = commentNotificationProxy;
    }

    public void publishComment(Comment comment) {
        commentRepository.storeComment(comment);
        commentNotificationProxy.sendComment(comment);
    }
}

In plain Java, Main has to build the whole graph itself — and that is exactly the code Spring will remove:

Main.javaListing 4.7 · manual wiring
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var commentRepository = new DBCommentRepository();
        var commentNotificationProxy = new EmailCommentNotificationProxy();

        var commentService = new CommentService(
                commentRepository, commentNotificationProxy);

        var comment = new Comment();
        comment.setAuthor("Laurentiu");
        comment.setText("Demo comment");

        commentService.publishComment(comment);
    }
}
ConsoleStoring comment: Demo comment Sending notification for comment: Demo comment
Section 4.2

Now let Spring do the wiring

Add spring-context, annotate three classes, and delete the object construction from Main.

4.2.1 — Which objects belong in the context?

The rule the book gives is a question: does this object need to be managed by the framework? For this app the only Spring feature in play is DI, so an object earns a place in the context if it has a dependency to inject or is a dependency of something else.

ClassBean?Why
CommentServiceYesIt has two dependencies that must be injected.
DBCommentRepositoryYesIt implements a contract and is a dependency of the service.
EmailCommentNotificationProxyYesSame — a dependency of the service.
CommentNoNo dependencies, and nothing needs it injected. Making it a bean would add complexity with no benefit.
CommentRepository, CommentNotificationProxyNoThey are interfaces; Spring cannot instantiate them. Stereotype annotations go on classes only.
The most common beginner mistake

Adding every object to the context. Beans exist so the framework can control and augment them; a bean Spring only holds and never touches just makes the app harder to maintain and slightly slower to start.

DBCommentRepository.javaListing 4.8
@Component
public class DBCommentRepository
        implements CommentRepository {

    @Override
    public void storeComment(Comment comment) {
        System.out.println("Storing comment: " + comment.getText());
    }
}
EmailCommentNotificationProxy.javaListing 4.9
@Component
public class EmailCommentNotificationProxy
        implements CommentNotificationProxy {

    @Override
    public void sendComment(Comment comment) {
        System.out.println("Sending notification for comment: "
                + comment.getText());
    }
}

The service keeps its constructor injection — but now the parameters are interfaces, and Spring is expected to find compatible beans. With a single constructor, @Autowired is optional.

services/CommentService.javaListing 4.10 · injection by contract
@Component
public class CommentService {

    private final CommentRepository commentRepository;
    private final CommentNotificationProxy commentNotificationProxy;

    public CommentService(CommentRepository commentRepository,
                          CommentNotificationProxy commentNotificationProxy) {
        this.commentRepository = commentRepository;
        this.commentNotificationProxy = commentNotificationProxy;
    }

    public void publishComment(Comment comment) {
        commentRepository.storeComment(comment);
        commentNotificationProxy.sendComment(comment);
    }
}
ProjectConfiguration.javaListing 4.11
@Configuration
@ComponentScan(basePackages = {
        "proxies", "services", "repositories"
})
public class ProjectConfiguration {
}
Main.javaListing 4.12 · no wiring code
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(
                ProjectConfiguration.class);

        var comment = new Comment();
        comment.setAuthor("Laurentiu");
        comment.setText("Demo comment");

        var commentService = context.getBean(CommentService.class);
        commentService.publishComment(comment);
    }
}

Same two lines of console output, and no new CommentService(...) anywhere. That deletion is the whole point: the object graph is described by annotations, not constructed by hand.

Packages or classes in @ComponentScan?

basePackages is one line even when a package holds twenty components — but a package rename can silently break the scan. basePackageClasses is more verbose yet survives renames with a compile error. The book finds both in production and does not declare a winner.

Section 4.2.2

When a contract has several implementations

Add a second notification channel and Spring refuses to guess — exactly as it did with several parrots in chapter 3.

CommentPushNotificationProxy.javaListing 4.13 · a second implementation
@Component
public class CommentPushNotificationProxy
        implements CommentNotificationProxy {

    @Override
    public void sendComment(Comment comment) {
        System.out.println("Sending push notification for comment: "
                + comment.getText());
    }
}
Exception · two candidates, no decisionCaused by: org.springframework.beans.factory.NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException: No qualifying bean of type 'proxies.CommentNotificationProxy' available: expected single matching bean but found 2: commentPushNotificationProxy,emailCommentNotificationProxy

Option 1 — @Primary

Mark one implementation as the default. This is also the book's recommended fix when a library already ships an implementation of an interface you need to replace with your own.

CommentPushNotificationProxy.javaListing 4.14 · default choice
@Component
@Primary
public class CommentPushNotificationProxy
        implements CommentNotificationProxy {
    // ...
}
Console · the push implementation wonStoring comment: Demo comment Sending push notification for comment: Demo comment

Option 2 — @Qualifier

When different objects genuinely need different implementations — email for audit, push for mentions — name the beans and ask for one by name.

Naming the two implementations@Qualifier on the bean
@Component
@Qualifier("PUSH")
public class CommentPushNotificationProxy
        implements CommentNotificationProxy {
    // ...
}

@Component
@Qualifier("EMAIL")
public class EmailCommentNotificationProxy
        implements CommentNotificationProxy {
    // ...
}
services/CommentService.javaListing 4.15 · choosing at the injection point
@Component
public class CommentService {

    private final CommentRepository commentRepository;
    private final CommentNotificationProxy commentNotificationProxy;

    public CommentService(
            CommentRepository commentRepository,
            @Qualifier("PUSH") CommentNotificationProxy commentNotificationProxy) {
        this.commentRepository = commentRepository;
        this.commentNotificationProxy = commentNotificationProxy;
    }

    // Omitted code
}
ProjectConfiguration.javaThe same thing with @Bean methods
@Configuration
public class ProjectConfiguration {

    @Bean
    public CommentRepository commentRepository() {
        return new DBCommentRepository();
    }

    @Bean
    public CommentNotificationProxy commentNotificationProxy() {
        return new EmailCommentNotificationProxy();
    }

    @Bean
    public CommentService commentService(CommentRepository commentRepository,
            CommentNotificationProxy commentNotificationProxy) {
        return new CommentService(commentRepository, commentNotificationProxy);
    }
}

Worth noticing: the @Bean methods take interface types as parameters, so auto-wiring works with abstractions exactly the same way. All three injection styles from chapter 3 — constructor, field, setter — behave identically here.

Section 4.3

Stereotypes that name the responsibility

@Component says "a bean". @Service and @Repository say "a bean, and here is its job".

All three annotations do the same technical thing: Spring creates an instance and adds it to the context. The difference is what a reader of the class learns in the first line. Since services and repositories are the two responsibilities that dominate real designs, Spring gives each a dedicated annotation.

services/CommentService.java@Service
@Service
public class CommentService {
    // Omitted code
}
repositories/DBCommentRepository.java@Repository
@Repository
public class DBCommentRepository
        implements CommentRepository {
    // Omitted code
}
A small honesty note

Technically the three are interchangeable — Spring treats them as components. @Repository additionally enables persistence-exception translation when used with Spring's data access support, and @Service is purely documentation. But documentation that every reader understands is not decoration: it is design made visible.

Recap

Chapter 4's summary, in plain sentences

Six sentences worth remembering

  • Decouple with abstractions. Depend on an interface so implementations can change without rippling through the app.
  • Interfaces are contracts. The interface declares the what; each implementation supplies the how.
  • Spring injects by contract. Ask for an interface and Spring finds a bean whose class implements it.
  • Annotate classes, never interfaces. Only classes can be instantiated.
  • Two implementations need a decision. Use @Primary for a default, or @Qualifier to choose by name.
  • Say what a bean does. @Service and @Repository keep the class design readable; @Component covers the rest.

What changed in your head

You have now seen the shape of a real Spring application: services orchestrating use cases, repositories persisting, proxies talking to the outside world — all connected through interfaces and injected by the framework. That is chapters 2, 3 and 4 combined, and it is the foundation the rest of the book builds on.
